clue.text: The state of some Cambridge fellows!

definitions.text: The state of some Cambridge fellows!

parts.words: The state of some Cambridge fellows!
parts.note: suggests dons of the English university town, but the fellows meant are at Harvard or MIT in the US city of Cambridge, so the state is the one that city lies in

explanation.surface: A remark on the condition of some Oxbridge academics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cambridge fellows' sends the mind to the English university; there is a second Cambridge, home of Harvard and MIT, in New England.
explanation.definitionFit: The American city of Cambridge lies in this New England state, so its residents and academics belong to it.

clue.text: Teacher digested words in many a novel

parts.note: a schoolmaster is a teacher

indicators.note: in means one word is placed within the other

parts.note: taken as written
having taken in written words is to have read them

explanation.surface: A schoolteacher absorbed the text of many a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'digested words' looks like a description of reading matter, but it is just the verb for taking in text. Captain Marryat's 1841 children's novel is about a shipwrecked family and their seaman.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Frederick Marryat wrote this 1841 children's book of shipwreck adventure.

clue.text: Energy needed to cook

definitions.meaning: vapour power, or vigour and drive, as in running out of puff
to cook food by vapour over boiling water

explanation.definitionFit: Water vapour drives engines and stands for vigour, and the verb means to cook over boiling water.

clue.text: Among opponents these are diametrically opposite

definitions.note: describes things that are opposites; the answer is the noun for such contrasts

indicators.note: among means one word sits within the other

parts.note: antis are people opposed to something
taken as written

explanation.surface: Within a group of opponents, some hold completely opposing views.
explanation.walkthrough: THESE goes among ANTIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Contrasts or direct opposites stand in complete opposition to each other.

clue.text: Integrity of good man embraced by sweetheart'

indicators.note: embraced by means held within the arms of the other word

parts.note: honey is a term of endearment for a sweetheart
ST, saint, is a crossword stock for a good man

explanation.surface: A virtuous man is hugged by his lover.
explanation.walkthrough: ST for saint is a crossword convention for a good man; 'embraced by' puts him inside the sweetheart.
explanation.definitionFit: Integrity is truthfulness and moral uprightness.

clue.text: Pugnacious type: on the picket line?

definitions.meaning: someone who hits out, a puncher
a worker withdrawing labour in an industrial dispute

explanation.definitionFit: One who hits out is a hitter, and a worker on picket duty has downed tools in a dispute.

clue.text: Member keeping master's book

indicators.note: keeping means holding something inside

parts.note: a toe is a member, a limb or part of the body
M is short for master

explanation.surface: A club member hanging on to the headmaster's book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' looks like a club member; a member is also a body part, here TOE, which keeps M inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A large, heavy volume is a weighty book.

clue.text: Lackey put a count in place

indicators.note: in means these letters go into the other word

parts.note: a site is a place
to tell is to count, as in telling beads or votes

explanation.surface: A servant installed a nobleman somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'count' looks like a nobleman but is the verb TELL; A and TELL go into SITE.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower or hanger-on who depends on a powerful patron, as a moon orbits a planet.

clue.text: New centre with two shops emitting light

indicators.note: new means the letters are made into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
two shops gives the word shop twice
two shops gives the word shop twice

explanation.surface: A new shopping centre containing a pair of stores, lit up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges CENTRE with SHOP and SHOP.
explanation.definitionFit: Glowing with a faint light, especially without heat, as some sea creatures do.

clue.text: Pudding Descartes rejected as a substitute for sugar

parts.note: a sweet is a British word for a pudding or dessert course

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the philosopher's first name is read backwards

parts.note: the French philosopher René Descartes, giving his first name

explanation.surface: A diner turning down a dessert in favour of something to sweeten a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pudding' is the British sense of any dessert. 'rejected' sends the philosopher's first name backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Saccharin or aspartame are additives used in place of sugar to give food a sweet taste.

clue.text: Test for a look-alike?

definitions.meaning: a Test is a full international cricket fixture, a contest between two sides
something that exactly resembles another, a perfect pair

explanation.definitionFit: A cricket Test is a game between teams, and a thing identical to another is its counterpart or equal.

clue.text: Half of them satisfied an old busybody

indicators.note: half of means the first two of the word's four letters are taken

parts.note: to have satisfied a need or demand is to have met it

explanation.surface: Only half of a group were content with a meddling old person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'busybody' looks like a nosy person, but here it is an ant, a famously busy creature; 'old' marks an archaic dialect word.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic and dialect word for an ant, an insect proverbial for being busy.

clue.text: Clovis's creator, up to his monkey tricks?

definitions.meaning: the pen name of H H Munro, whose short stories feature the mischievous Clovis Sangrail
a South American monkey with a bushy tail

explanation.surface: An author, playful as ever, getting up to mischief.
explanation.definitionFit: H H Munro wrote under this pen name, which is also the name of a South American primate.

clue.text: Advantage examinees once had after eleven

definitions.meaning: a benefit or positive point in one's favour
the eleven-... was the exam English children once sat at the end of primary school to decide their secondary school

explanation.surface: A head start that pupils used to get once they passed eleven.
explanation.walkthrough: The 11-plus was a British selective exam taken around age eleven, which decided entry to grammar schools.
explanation.definitionFit: A benefit is a positive point, and the old British selection exam was called the eleven-something.

clue.text: Subsequently establish protégé in course

indicators.note: in means one word is put inside the other

parts.note: afters is a British word for the dessert course
a ward is a young person under a guardian's protection

explanation.surface: Later, set up a favourite on a training course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'course' looks like a course of study, but it is the British word for the dessert course; 'establish' just links the parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Subsequently means at a later time, following something.

clue.text: "The Riddle of the Ancient Guild"

definitions.meaning: an enigma or puzzle that is hard to explain
in medieval usage a craft or trade guild, as in the guild plays of the Middle Ages

explanation.surface: Looks like the title of a detective novel about an old trade society.
explanation.walkthrough: The medieval sense of a trade guild survives in the name of the mystery plays the guilds staged.
explanation.definitionFit: An enigma is something unexplained, and in the Middle Ages the word also meant a craft guild.

clue.text: Englishman's ship in North Sea. storm starts to alter course hurriedly

indicators.note: in means one piece goes inside the other
a storm whips things up, so these letters are tossed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
SS is steamship

indicators.note: starts means the first letters of the following words

explanation.surface: An English vessel in a North Sea gale changes course quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'storm' rearranges NSEA as SAEN; 'in' puts the ship inside; 'starts to' takes the first letters of the last three words. It is the Scots term for an English person.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish and Irish term, often mildly hostile, for a person from England.

clue.text: Dissipated like some servicemen, say?

definitions.meaning: a punning reading: resembling the Royal Air Force would be RAF-ish, and 'say' signals the coined word is pronounced like a real one

explanation.walkthrough: The RAF is Britain's Royal Air Force.
explanation.definitionFit: Raffish means disreputable or rakish, the manner of someone who leads a dissolute, debauched life.

clue.text: Obtains, inside information in return for sum of money

indicators.note: in return means the whole assembled string of letters is read backwards
inside means one word sits within the other

parts.note: gen is British slang for information
obtains means gets

explanation.surface: Someone acquires inside knowledge in exchange for cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside information' looks like one phrase but is split: 'inside' puts the verb within the slang for information, and 'in return' reverses the whole thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Savings put aside for the future are a reserve fund of cash kept safe like an egg in a nest.

clue.text: Spanish nobleman's horse carrying money in South Africa

indicators.note: carrying means holding the other word within

parts.note: gee, or gee-gee, is a child's word for a horse
the rand is the currency of South Africa

explanation.surface: A Spanish aristocrat's horse transports cash in South Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carrying' puts the South African currency within the child's word for a horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A Spanish or Portuguese aristocrat of the highest rank.

clue.text: Woman speculator, or Kipling's more deadly female?

parts.note: she is a pronoun standing for a woman
a bear is a stock-market speculator who sells expecting prices to fall

explanation.surface: Either a female stock trader or the deadly woman of Kipling's poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's poem 'The Female of the Species' says the female of a large wild animal of the woods is more deadly than the male.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling's poem cites the female of this forest animal, met on the trail, as deadlier than the male.

clue.text: Strain caused by a term of imprisonment

definitions.meaning: to pull or extend something tight
slang for a spell in jail

explanation.definitionFit: Pulling something taut is to extend it, and a jail sentence is slang for a period served.

clue.text: Blade for cutting off entrance to tent

indicators.note: the entrance to a word is its first letter, and cutting it off removes it

parts.note: a tepee is a conical tent of the Plains peoples

explanation.surface: A knife used to slash the opening of a tent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entrance' looks like a tent flap, but it means the first letter of TEPEE.
explanation.definitionFit: A fencing sword with a stiff, narrow blade, used in competitive swordplay.

clue.text: Just a swallow by a tree

indicators.note: to be swallowed by something is to end up inside it

parts.note: a fir is a coniferous tree

explanation.surface: Merely a small bird perched next to a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swallow' looks like the bird, but it is the instruction that A goes inside FIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Just means equitable and even-handed, treating all sides impartially.

clue.text: Saleable items used to be worn by soldiers

indicators.note: something worn by a person is held around them, so one word wraps the other

parts.note: used to be means was
RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps

explanation.surface: Goods for sale that soldiers once wore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worn by' puts the abbreviation for the Royal Engineers, a British army corps, inside the past tense.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods offered for sale are merchandise or stock a trader sells.

clue.text: The strap is said thus to prevail

indicators.note: is said means the word is spoken and heard as another

parts.note: a rein is a strap used to guide a horse

explanation.surface: A belt is said to be the way to get the upper hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The strap' is REIN, the horse's strap.
explanation.definitionFit: To rule or hold sway is to predominate, to be in power.

clue.text: Way an artist rises to be a celebrity

parts.note: ST is short for street, a way

indicators.note: rises means the letters go upwards, read backwards in a down clue

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: How a painter climbs to fame.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'rises' reads the artist's letters upwards, so backwards; RA (Royal Academician) is a crossword stock for an artist.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous performer is someone at the top, a big name.

clue.text: Military detachment found way back towards the stern

indicators.note: back means the abbreviation is read in reverse

parts.note: RD is short for road, a way
aft is the nautical direction towards the rear of a ship

explanation.surface: A unit of troops discovered a route back to the rear of the ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the road abbreviation round; 'aft' is the sailor's word for the rear.
explanation.definitionFit: A group of troops detached and sent off for a duty is a draught or detail.

clue.text: Resolve to make boy return fur

indicators.note: return means the boy's name is read backwards

parts.note: Ted, a common boy's name
ermine is the white winter fur of the stoat

explanation.surface: A determination to have a boy give back a fur.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' reads the boy's name backwards; ermine is the stoat's white winter coat.
explanation.definitionFit: To resolve is to decide or settle firmly on something.

clue.text: Before tea, say, there's no such mixed fruit

indicators.note: before means the scrambled letters come ahead of the next piece
mixed means the letters of the words there's no such are scrambled
say means the word is heard, giving its letter name

parts.note: tea sounds like the letter T

explanation.surface: A claim that a particular fruit doesn't exist, made at teatime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixed' rearranges 'there's no such' into the first twelve letters, which come 'Before' the letter heard in 'tea, say'. 'Before tea' suggests an afternoon scene.
explanation.definitionFit: The glossy brown nut of the conker tree is the seed of a large ornamental tree, loosely called its fruit.
